item.title: Dune vs Opam vs Esy in 2026: Which OCaml Build Toolchain Should You Actually Use?
item.description: OCaml teams lose more hours to build plumbing than to the type system. A fresh clone that takes 40 minutes to compile, a CI job that passes locally and fails on the runner because someone’s opam switch had a different dune binary, or a monorepo where the formatter version silently rewrote 300 files — these are toolchain problems, not language problems. And the OCaml toolchain is unusual among modern ecosystems: two package managers and one build system coexist, and they are not interchangeable.

item.title: wasm-tools vs wit-bindgen vs WAC in 2026: Building WASI Components That Actually Ship
item.description: WebAssembly’s component model stopped being a research demo somewhere in 2025. The problem is that the documentation never caught up: a newcomer runs cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, ships a .wasm file, and discovers that nobody can call it — because it exports a memory blob, not a typed interface. The gap between “a Wasm module exists” and “a component with a versioned interface that a host can link” is exactly where three command-line tools live: wasm-tools, wit-bindgen, and wac.

item.title: GnuCOBOL vs SuperBOL vs COBOL Check in 2026: The Complete Open-Source COBOL Toolchain Compared
item.description: There are still an estimated 200+ billion lines of COBOL running the world’s banking, insurance, and airline systems — and the average COBOL developer is over 45. The language is not the bottleneck anymore. The toolchain is. Compilers that only build on z/OS, editors with no autocomplete, and zero unit test infrastructure are what actually slow legacy teams down.

item.title: The Definitive Guide to the Zig Toolchain in 2026: zig build, ZLS, and zig cc Compared
item.description: Here is the fact that should get your attention: zig cc is a fully working C and C++ cross-compiler for 12+ targets, and it ships inside a single ~45 MB tarball with zero external dependencies. No gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu package. No sysroot tarballs. No Docker image full of cross toolchains. You download Zig, and thirty seconds later you are producing static RISC-V binaries on an x86 host.

item.title: Self-Hosted Project Scaffolding & Code Generation: Cookiecutter vs Yeoman vs Plop vs Hygen
item.description:
Introduction

Every software project starts the same way: create directories, write boilerplate, configure linters, set up CI/CD, add Docker files. This repetitive setup work — the “project scaffolding” phase — consumes hours that could be spent on actual feature development. Code generation and scaffolding tools automate this grunt work, letting teams spin up production-ready project structures in seconds rather than hours.
